## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Its primary function is the systematic classification of disciplinary transgressions according to their origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), defining how offenses arise through the specific channels of body, speech, or mind.

No direct external parallels in Chinese, Tibetan, or Sanskrit traditions are recorded for this chapter, and DharmaNexus identifies no cross-language alignments with significant similarity [DharmaNexus]. Internally, however, DharmaNexus highlights intense textual reuse within the Pali canon, registering 221 matching segments across 23 texts [DharmaNexus]. These matches reflect shared analytical schemes and repeating Vinaya formulas found across other sections of the *Parivāra*, most notably the *Katthapaññattivāra* (Pvr 1.1 and Pvr 2.1), *Antarapeyyāla* (Pvr 4), *Atthāpattisamuṭṭhāna* (Pvr 18), *Samuccayavāra* (Pvr 2.8 and Pvr 2.16), and corresponding *Samuṭṭhānavāra* treatments (Pvr 1.5, Pvr 1.13, and Pvr 2.13) [DharmaNexus].

*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on catalog and DharmaNexus data.*
